text.p: International Business Machines Corp. reported a better-than-expected first-quarter profit of $1.19 billion, citing strength in rapidly growing businesses like personal computers and services.
The profit, equal to $2.37 a share, compared with first-quarter earnings of $1.20 billion, or $2.21 a share a year earlier, when IBM had more shares outstanding.
The 1996 results excluded a charge for acquisitons. Including the charge, IBM had earnings of $774 million, or $1.41 a share a year ago.
The results beat the consensus Wall Street analyst forecast of $2.28 a share, according to the First Call service. Predictions had ranged from $2.10 to $2.37.
Revenues rose 5 percent to $17.3 billion from $16.6 billion in last year's quarter.

"We continued to see strong performance in the first quarter in fast-growth areas, including services, personal computers and certain ... software such as Lotus Notes and Tivoli systems management products," IBM Chairman Louis Gerstner said in a statement.
Gerstner said the results from those businesses more than offset weakness in mainframes, minicomputers and workstations.

Overall hardware sales totalled $7.8 billion, essentially flat compared with the previous year. Revenues from services jumped 28 percent to $4.1 billion and overall software revenues declined 3 percent to $2.9 billion.
IBM said revenues outside the United States were dragged down by the strong dollar.

North America turned in the strongest performance, with revenues increasing 14 percent to $7.9 billion, the company said. Revenues from the Asia-Pacific region rose 3 percent to $3.4 billion and Latin America's contribution edged up 2 percent to $701 million.
Revenues from Europe, the Middle East and Africa declined 7 percent to $5.3 billion.
Had it not been for the strong dollar, the Asia-Pacific region's revenues would have grown 14 percent, while revenue from Europe, the Middle East and Africa would have risen 1 percent.
IBM stock rose $2.375 to $142.375 in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange in anticipation of the Armonk, N.Y.-based computer power's earnings report.

IBM again reported earnings after the stock market closed, a routine it adopted last quarter, to avoid some of the volatility in its stock during its meeting and conference call with analysts, which was to begin at 4:30 p.m. EDT.
